title: How Retrieval and Reranking works in RAG | Bi Encoder vs Cross Encoder
description:
In this video we explore the difference between bi encoders and cross encoders.
Bi encoders are primarily used as embedding model in a retriever while cross encoders are mainly used as reranking model in a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) flow.

1:29 Cross Encoder
2:36 Bi Encoder
3:27 Differences between bi encoders and cross encoders
4:01 Code Snippets for bi encoders and cross encoders

transcript.text:
Retrieval and reranking are two important 
concepts in the RAG workflow. But how do

they actually work and why is there a need to 
use reranking models to rank context passages

again after retrieval? That's what we'll be 
exploring in this video. We would be focusing

on embedding using BERT based bi-encoder and 
ranking using BERT based cross encoders. On a

high level embedding models are typically used for 
creating embeddings of documents and queries both

in the vector store creation and context retrieval 
stage, while reranking models are typically used

to rerank context passages post the context 
retrieval stage. Embedding models can be used

for creating embeddings as well as determining the 
similarity score but ranking models can only help

with determining the similarity score. BERT model 
uses the same Transformer architecture outlined in

the paper Attention is all you need. A Transformer 
model comprises of an encoder and a decoder. If

you would need the numerical representation 
of a passage of text, you would simply use

the pooled output of the BERT Model. A BERT model 
is simply a bidirectional multi-layer Transformer

encoder. This output embedding represents the 
semantics as well as other aspects of the piece

of text as a whole in the n dimensional 
space. Here n is the size of the embedding

A BERT based cross encoder model accepts a pair 
of text and determines the degree of similarity

between them using a binary classification head. 
Given a query and document, it first tokenizes

them. Then they are merged together separated by 
the SEP token. The input embeddings corresponding

to the tokens are then fed to the BERT model. The 
pooled output of the BERT model is finally passed

on to the binary classification layer. The output 
of the binary classification layer lies in the

range 0 and 1 and it is a measure of the semantic 
similarity between the query and the document.

There are token level interactions between the 
query and the passage which contributes to its

high accuracy in determining semantic similarity. 
But there is an issue here. If we have a long

document and we want to get the passages 
most semantically similar to a given query,

we would have to pass all the query passage 
pairs at runtime for the entire document. This

would lead to poor latency if used on real time 
applications and also lead to high computational

cost. This is where buy encoder comes in. Here 
queries and passages are processed separately,

so we don't need to pass them in pairs 
just like in Cross encoders. A given

piece of text is tokenized and passed to a 
BERT model. Mean pooling is then applied,

finally after normalization we get the output 
embeddings corresponding to the input text
Now if we have a query and a passage, we can find

out their degree of semantic similarity 
by using cosine similarity over both the

embeddings. If we have a query and two passages, 
we can find out which passage is most semantically

similar by comparing the cosine similarity 
scores of both the passages with the query.

So in bi-encoders, accuracy of semantic similarity 
matching is slightly reduced due to the absence of

token level interactions between the query 
and the passages. But on a brighter side,

passages can be processed separately, and 
the embeddings can be stored beforehand.

For a given query we can retrieve the passage 
most semantically similar using the cosine

similarity operation. Since the passages needs 
to be processed just once, similarity matching

is less computationally expensive compared 
to cross encoders. You can try out cross

encoder and bi encoder models using both sentence 
Transformer library as well as through Langchain

Significant attempts have been made to 
bridge the gap between cross encoders

and bi encoders. This paper introduces 
the concept of late interactions. Instead

of compressing the entire passage into 
a single vector embedding, it proposes

token level embeddings. Similarity 
match is performed using the MaxSim

operation. This paper on the other hand proposes 
training strategies for shallow cross encoders.

A shallow cross encoder would have less number 
of layers than a full-sized BERT model and their

latency on retrieval task would be much better. 
These would be covered in much more detail in

my upcoming videos. So that's it for this video. 
Hope you like it. Let's learn and grow together
